new_statements.rule_in_words: Lubwisi is analysed as a two-tone (H vs L) Bantu tone language: lexical minimal pairs differ only in tone (Spelling Guide p. 24: [kʊ̀kɔ́mà] 'to go up' vs [kʊ̀kɔ̀mà] 'to pick, choose'), every vowel bears H or L, all four tonal patterns occur on disyllabic noun roots, verb roots are H or L with toneless extensions, and H is downstepped after L. Neither the survey nor the spelling guide makes any statement about word stress, accent position, or penultimate prominence; the section heading 'Tone or accent' is the SIL template heading and the content is purely tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal details only: rare H noun prefixes (3 of >1,000 nouns, p. 36); final vowel of CVC-root infinitives utterance-finally always L (p. 37); polar tones in imperatives; non-phonemic glottal stop on utterance-final H syllable (p. 4). No stress exceptions because no stress claim.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone, illustrated with citation forms (infinitives, prefixed nouns) and some inflected verb forms; downstep described across the word. No phrase-level or intonational statement bearing on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both downloaded sources describe the LuBwisi (Bwisi) variety spoken in Bwamba County, Bundibugyo District, Uganda (informant from Busunga, Bubandi sub-county); the Congolese variety Kitalinga (Butalinga, Beni, North Kivu) is the object of Paluku 1998 and Sindani 1986. Tabb (p. 46) treats KiTalinga and LuBwisi as dialects of one language (Glottolog tali1258 has no dialect-level codes); he notes one phonological difference of analysis (Paluku: vowel length not distinctive in Kitalinga; Tabb: length contrastive in Lubwisi).

sources.locator: Section 7 'Tone or accent', pp. 36-37 (PDF pp. 36-37); supporting statement in Lubwisi Spelling Guide 3rd ed. (2011) p. 24
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Section 7 'Tone or accent' (pp. 36-38) describes a two-tone (H/L) system with minimal pairs contrasting only in tone, one tone per vowel, all four tone patterns on disyllabic noun roots, H or L CVC verb roots with toneless extensions, downstepped H after L, polar tones in imperatives; p. 4 notes a non-phonemic glottal stop on an utterance-final high-tone syllable. Syllable (§3) and word-structure (§4) sections say nothing about prominence or penultimate lengthening.
